cells.tense: Right now you are holding a seed — something concrete that's ready to begin.
cells.ask: Pick the one thing worth your attention, start the rough version today, and let it grow without forcing the pace.
cells.core:
You have something new in your hands, and you're holding it the way it wants to be held. You see what it needs and you give it that, not everything. The seed doesn't need proving or forcing. It needs someone to keep turning toward it, and you're doing that.

The sign that this is going well is small and plain: a thing gets your attention, you pick it up, and nothing has to be settled first. You're not standing off to the side waiting. You're in the work, choosing what to feed it and how much, and you can rest while it grows. Holding it this way contains what's there rather than crushing it, and that's the whole job.
cells.sheetLine: You know what this needs and you're letting it grow at its own pace.
cells.verb: holding the seed of what's taking form
cells.place: in the place that knows what's worth attending to

cells.tense: You will work out how this turns out before anyone would know — even you.
cells.ask: At the next decision point, act before the plan settles. Let one thing happen before you're certain what it will be.
cells.core:
There's something small in front of you and you've raced ahead of it. You're already forecasting the outcome, arranging the next five steps, testing whether the seed was worth planting. Your attention isn't on what's actually here — it's on a version that doesn't exist yet and keeps refusing to be pinned down.

When the attention is working right it stays small: notice the thing, pick it up, begin. Instead it has turned into planning, and you're using it to secure a future rather than read the present. The seed gets less air that way. The load you're carrying is real, but it's the hypothetical version, and the actual thing is being crowded out.
cells.sheetLine: You've cast this forward so far you've left the actual seed behind.
cells.verb: holding the seed of what's taking form

cells.tense: Something was ready to begin and you were looking at a door that's already behind you.
cells.ask: Find one practical thing almost in reach today and begin it badly, without waiting for a signal to confirm it.
cells.core:
When this is working, it's small and ordinary. A thing in front of you gets attended to, you pick it up, you begin. There's no announcement and no certainty first. The seed gets carried because someone decided to carry it, and deciding was enough.

What's happening instead is that the beginning keeps getting postponed. You keep checking whether you know enough yet, waiting for a clear signal from inside, and the signal isn't coming, so the thing sits. From outside it looks like patience. What's absent is the start, not the recognition. Waiting doesn't charge what's starved of motion, and only motion feeds it.
cells.sheetLine: You keep checking whether you know enough, and knowing isn't fed by motion.

cells.tense: You are already holding the seed steady, and talking about it as though luck or timing did the holding.
cells.ask: Name one thing worth your attention and say out loud that it's your call — one sentence, no hedging.
cells.core:
Somewhere in this, you looked at a thing and knew it mattered. You gave it your attention when others glanced past it, and that's why it's still here. You've been calling it circumstance, or the right timing, or just that it landed in your lap. Nothing landed on its own. You kept returning to it, and returning is a thing a person does.

When this is owned, it's plain: attention given, and the act of choosing named. No category needed, no argument. One sentence that says this is mine and the choice was mine. That choice already happened. The saying-so is the part that's missing, and it's short.
cells.sheetLine: You noticed the thing worth noticing, but you're still calling it circumstance.

attempts.check: The unsupported claim is that the card's 'human seed' refers to a person — someone the reader is bringing into form. The record says the seed is a resource, opportunity, or material commitment presenting itself; the draw may well be a project, not a child. A reader could reasonably say 'the card was about an idea I've been circling, not a person.' The ask still works if the read is wrong: starting the ugly version today and watching what carries is usable whichever seed it is. The sentence serving the writer is any variant of 'you already know what it is' — it sounds like a promise and dodges the actual discernment work.
